utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please stand, and if you could read aloud the affirmation shown to you on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. I think Mr. Djordjevic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before we start with the examination-in-chief, I would like to warn you to make an effort, since we speak the same language, and considered that everything I will be examining you about today is interpreted into other languages, and that the interpreters need some time to interpret what I -- what I ask and then what you answer. There should be a pause between my question and your answer to enable the interpreters to interpret everything that is said. Please bear that in mind. Tell us your first and last name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Danica Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of April, 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Brod, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Macedonian by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you on the 25th of February, 2008, give a statement to Mr. Djordjevic's [as interpreted] Defence counsel -- Mr. Lukic and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The second name escaped us. Could counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The number of the statement is D007-2736. Let me first ask you, during the proofing for this examination, did you have an opportunity to review the statement that you gave to Mr. Lukic and Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue with the examination, I must point out that on page 2, line 12, it isn't Mr. Djordjevic's Defence counsel, but Mr. Lukic's Defence. That's page 2, line 12. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat everything you said then if you were asked the same questions today in that statement?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00853.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you testify in the Milutinovic the et al. case before this Tribunal on the 29th of February, 2008, and on the 4th of March, 2008?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to review that transcript during the proofing?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This being the case, would you today repeat everything that you stated during your evidence in that trial?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is Defence Exhibit D010-4044. I seek to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00854.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter summary, the 65 ter summary is as follows: The witness was an investigative judge of the district court of Pristina during the relevant period of time. She will testify to the structure and functioning of the judicial organs in Serbia during the relevant time-period and prior to that time. She will -- she will also testify about investigation procedure under the Law of Criminal Procedure that was in force at the time, but also about the Criminal Code of Serbia and that of Yugoslavia. She will give evidence about the judicial bodies functioning as independent bodies. Ms. Marinkovic will also speak about rulings passed by the district court in Pristina against criminal groups for war crimes and terrorism as well as acts directed against the constitutional assistant of Yugoslavia. She will also give evidence about her personal knowledge of investigations carried out into terrorists acts and crimes committed by the KLA and other armed groups against the state, the police, the army, as well as citizens of Albanian ethnicity and other ethnicities. Those investigations were conducted both before and during the NATO bombing campaign. She will also give evidence about her personal knowledge about other investigations conducted into crimes including her attendance and participation in the investigations of the Racak incident from 15 through 18 January 1999. The witness will explain everything that happened during her meeting with General Drewienkiewicz and about other events at the police station in Stimlje. She will testify about her meeting with General Vlastimir Djordjevic who stands accused here, as well as what she knows about the activities of Ambassador William Walker on the 16th of January, 1999, in the village of Racak. We will hear from the witness who was with her at that on-site investigation, as well as the forensic findings with regard to the bodies found in the mosque in Racak that involved a pathologist from Belarus and Finland. She will testify about the assistance of and duty held by the police in all these investigations, and she will also speak about the difficulties in these investigations due to the attacks by the KLA and NATO bombings. She will testify as to the Prosecution individuals, including the police for crimes committed in the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija. She will also testify about any investigation of specific incidents of the indictment that are personally known to her in the jurisdiction of the district court of Pristina. She will give evidence about the general situation in the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija in the relevant time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Marinkovic, you were born in Bosanski Brod. Tell me, did you go to school there or did it happen otherwise, because that town is today in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was only born in Bosanski Brod because my mother was born there and lived there. I went to school in Skopje in the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How did your education go?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from primary and secondary school as well as from the faculty of law in Skopje in the Republic of Macedonia, and all my education was in the Macedonian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: After graduating from the faculty of law on the 1st of March, 1975, I started working as a judge trainee at the municipal court in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In which department of the court did you work? Did you deal with specific issues, special issues, or did you work on all sorts of cases?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: As a judge trainee, I worked in the registry, in the administration, and I worked in the various departments. I first worked with a judge who worked on civil lawsuits, and later on I worked with a judge who worked on the criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: After nine months as a judge trainee or intern with the municipal court in Skopje, I continued my internship in the commercial court in Pristina. That was in September 1976 when I moved to Pristina with my family because I had married Stefan Marinkovic who was born in Pristina and who lived and worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you work as an intern at the commercial court in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. As an intern at the commercial court in Pristina, I worked for another few months in order to complete my internship of 12 months. After that, I -- all the requirements were fulfilled to apply for a state examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you examined?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in June 1976, and I passed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: After I had passed my examination in September 1976, I started working as an expert collaborator with the Supreme Court of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija, and my specialisation was administrative lawsuits, administrative law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And how about the continuation of your career, what about it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: As an expert collaborator, I stayed until July 1984 with the Supreme Court when I was selected to be a judge of the district court in Pristina where I continued working.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And how did your career develop after 1984?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: At the district court in Pristina, I stayed until 1999 when we had to leave Kosovo and Metohija. I left Pristina in June 1999 and continued working with the district court in Kragujevac where I worked as a judge until December 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like to know what exactly you did at the district court in Pristina, what -- which area of law did you deal with, until the time you left Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Once I was appointed judge of the district court in Pristina, I first started working on civilian lawsuits. I was a judge, an individual judge where I dealt with lawsuits, civil lawsuits from damages to all other sorts of matters of civil law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: As a judge in civil lawsuits, I worked until November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: After that the president of the court appointed me as an investigative judge at the district court in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And from that point on did you only do investigations, or did you also have other duties until 1999?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Until 1999 I worked as an investigative judge mostly, and sometimes I was also a member of the criminal trial chamber of the first instance when I was appointed to be a member of such trial chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you worked at the district court in Kragujevac until the 31st of December, 2009. What is your status today?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Currently I'm without a concrete assignment because in the first round of reappointment of judges I wasn't reappointed. Meanwhile, I applied in the second round, and I hope to be appointed again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this, now that we've heard your biographical information, the Defence will like to hear about the appointment of judges. How did these things go when you were appointed judge in 1984? What was the practice at the time in this Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? How were judges appointed specifically in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The appointment of judges [as interpreted] in the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija went as follows, the Assembly or parliament of the autonomous province appointed judges. As far as the then Yugoslavia is concerned, the appointment of judges in Kosovo and Metohija was specific in that an important element was whether there were vacancies in specific courts and who will be appointed because it mattered whether the vacant post was for a judge of Albanian ethnicity or a judge of another ethnicity. I'm saying this because at the time when I ran for the post of judge, there were two vacancies at the district court of Pristina. One was for an Albanian and the other for a non-Albanian. So that there was no specific time-frame for applications, but as soon as a post became vacant, it was -- that fact was published and the commission of the parliament considered the applications, and upon the proposal of that commission, the parliament selected judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have remark to the interpretation. It starts on page 8, line 13. It says the appointment of judges. What was meant was actually the selection of judges. I believe that you understand what I mean, Witness, and therefore my question is as follows: There's the selection and the appointment of judges. What is the difference? Can you explain that to us. What is the selection and what is the appointment of judges?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The selection of judges is the following: When parliament selects somebody to be a judge and after being selected, the candidates are sworn in. After that they are appointed as judges and can start working.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's much clearer. Can you please explain on the basis of what procedure the Assembly selects judges, what happens before a judge is selected? Does someone announce a vacancy, a calling on interested parties to apply for the job? What happens?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Before judges are selected, a vacancy is announced in the newspapers. The number of posts and for what rank of court is listed as are the criteria a candidate has to meet in order to be considered for the post of judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is the following: Once a person is selected as a judge of a certain court, whether a municipal or district court, is that person then selected to carry out a certain task, or are special tasks assigned only at a later stage, and if this is the case, if the former is the case, who decides which judge is to do what? What was the system in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: When a judge is selected by the Assembly, that person is selected only as a judge in general. After that the president of the court to which the judge has been selected draws up an annual plan signing particular assignments, particular jobs to each particular judge. So when a judge is selected, the person is selected to be a judge in general, not a particular kind of judge performing a particular kind of job.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 1994 you were assigned investigations, and only in some cases were you a member of a trial chamber. Was that decision made by the president of the court?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that decision was made by the president of that court. In that year, he assigned me to the post of investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the years preceding the outbreak of the conflict, you were a judge of the district court in Pristina. Can you tell me what the ethnic makeup of that court was at that time. So let's look at the period preceding this time. You said you were selected to the district court in 1984, so what was the ethnic composition then, and how did it change, if at all? We have the amendments and the constitution that followed in later years so that's why I'm asking you this so that we can draw parallels.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: When I was selected to be a judge of the district court in Pristina in 1984, the ethnic makeup in that court was such that most of the judges in that court were Albanians. I can't recall the precise numbers but between 85 and 90 per cent of the judges were Albanians. As an example, I can tell you that out of four investigating judges at that time, one was a Serb, three were Albanians. The trial chamber had one judge who was not an Albanian and the other three were Albanians. As for civil suits, where I worked, that was a mixed chamber. One judge was Albanian, one was a Croat, I was a Macedonian in that chamber, and there was one colleague who was Turkish by ethnicity. The remaining judges were all Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In that period until 1994 when you became an investigating judge, were there any changes as regarding the reappointment of judges or re-selection?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In the period up to 1994, there were no changes as regards the kind of court, but when in 1990 Serbia adopted a new constitution, there was a general re-selection of judges all over Serbia. I would like to add the following: Before the new constitution was adopted and the general re-selection of judges announced, judges were selected for an eight-year term of office. After the adoption of the new constitution in 1990 and the re-selection of judges in 1992, judges were appointed for a permanent tenure. There was no time-limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And can you describe the re-selection process in your court, the one where you worked?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the re-selection of judges in the Pristina district court, vacancies were announced, as was the case with all the courts in Serbia, and all those who considered that they met the criteria applied. There were no preconditions or preset criteria, apart from the fact that each candidate had to have graduated from the faculty of law, they had to have passed the exam for judges, and they had to have the bar exam. So they had to have the appropriate qualifications. All of us who applied for the district court in Pristina, both Albanians and candidates of other ethnicities were selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many Albanians applied for the post of judge of the Pristina district court, and did they all take the oath and start working as judges?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The candidates applying for those posts included four Albanians, to the best of my recollection, and all of them were selected. There was one colleague who was of Turkish ethnicity who was selected, but did not take the oath and was not appointed a judge of the district court, and there was another colleague who was of Muslim ethnicity and she, too, was selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there other judges who did not take the oath?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: A number of judges, to the best of my knowledge, were selected for the district court in Pristina. These were Albanians, but although they had been selected, they did not take the oath. They did not turn up. And they did not then continue working as judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, tell me, do you remember that at that time or after that time while you were still in Pristina up to 1999, taking into account that you are a Macedonian by ethnicity, someone asked you to sign a sort of declaration of loyalty to the authorities of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that at that time no one asked me to sign anything of that sort, anything about loyalty to the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you now more specific questions about your department, the investigative judges department in 1994. Can you tell us how many people were involved in these investigations, what was the number of judges, what the ethnic composition was, gender equality. So tell us everything you can about this in the period from 1994 when you became an investigating judge to the time when you left Kosovo and Metohija in 1995, for well known reasons.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1994 when I began working as an investigating judge in the district court in Pristina, there were four investigating judges. Whenever it was possible, that was the number of judges that were supposed to be working on investigations. In 1994 there was myself, an Albanian colleague and two colleagues who were Serbs. This was the case until 1997, the beginning or middle of 1997. I can't remember precisely. At that time a colleague was re-assigned by the president of the court to the criminal trial chamber and another colleague was re-assigned by the president of the court who was authorised to do this to fill the post of acting president of the municipal court in Pristina, so that my colleague who was an Albanian and myself covered all the investigating work. In the course of 1998, a new judge was selected and the president assigned him to the investigations department to be an investigating judge. And towards the end of 1998, the colleague who had been acting president of the municipal court in Pristina returned and continued working as an investigating judge, so that until the NATO air-strikes, there were four of us, four investigating judges, that is. When the NATO air-strikes began, a colleague was called upon to be a judge of the military court, the Albanian colleague was forced for security reasons to avoid him and his family being killed by the KLA to leave Pristina with his family, so that I and another colleague remained covering all investigations in the course of the NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And to round off this topic, could you try to compare the workload you had just before the NATO air-strikes and during the NATO air-strikes. Was the workload the same, was it more or less, before or after, and if so, how much more or less? Can you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1997 and 1998 the workload in the investigations increased because there were frequent terrorist attacks, both against civilians, Albanian and non-Albanian, and against police officers, soldiers, buildings where state institutions were located, so that there were many investigations for -- in cases where there was terrorism or a conspiracy to engage in hostile activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us to what extent the workload increased because I believe you told us that there were only two investigating judges working in that period instead of the usual four. So how were your duties organised, your duty shifts and so on?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, during the air-strikes, the workload increased even more. We had our regular work, and in view of the fact that NATO began bombing civilian facilities where we were the court that had jurisdiction, we had to go and carry out on-site investigations. There were also investigations conducted against Albanians who were charged with a crime of conspiracy to engage in hostile activities and terrorism. So we worked under very difficult conditions. We spent more time at work than we did at home, and the security situation was very bad. We had constant air-raid warnings. We were constantly under stress and in fear, but we tried to keep everything under control, and as regards urgent cases in the court, to carry out all our duties in compliance with the law. When the NATO air-strikes began, a number of judges who had young children were relieved of their work duty, and they left Pristina with their children and their families in order to protect themselves both from the NATO air-strikes and from the terrorist activities that frequently occurred in Pristina. Many employees left the court so that our work was carried on under very difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We will now move on to a topic which I think we have to deal with briefly, and it has to do with the procedure of investigations since most of those familiar with common law are not familiar with the procedures followed at that time in the FRY, that's why I feel it necessary to throw some light on that part of your activity in order to clarify to all those in the courtroom what rules and principles were followed. Please tell us what process law applied at that time as regards criminal cases. What law were you guided by?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure. We refer to it by the acronym ZKP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was it a federal law, a republican law, or a law that applied in the province of Kosovo, a provincial law?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a federal law which applied on the entire territory of the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 65 ter 1824 on the screen, please. Or D011 -- yes, this is it. Can we see the English version. Could we please see Article 157. That should be around page 30 of the original, and as for the English version ... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that Articles 157 and the following articles deal with preliminary examination. Do take a look at that article or any article that you know better. I believe that goes until Article 181.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The law that we are looking at now, until what time was it applied?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was applied until 2001. In 2001 or 2002 the Republican Law on Criminal Procedure was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So this law was applied in the relevant time-period from May to June 1999?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, since we are talking about the FRY, the continental system of criminal law was applied. Do explain to us the section of the law that speaks about preliminary examination and what were the duties of the investigating judge, what was the procedure like?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to provide an answer to that question, I will need some time. I will have to be -- it will have to be a longer answer. Under the Law on Criminal Procedure, an investigation is launched against a certain person if there is found a suspicion that the person has committed a crime. The investigation is conducted based on a request of the authorised public prosecutor who files a request to the president of the court that an investigation be launched, and such an investigation is mandatory for every crime that is punishable with five years of imprisonment or more. The case files submitted by the prosecutor the investigating judge is reviewed, and then the investigating judge will decide whether the investigation will be launched or continued, but before that decision is taken on conducting an investigation or preliminary examination, the investigating judge is duty-bound to interview the suspect or the accused. Once the decision on conducting a preliminary examination is taken, the investigating judge, during the preliminary examination, collects evidence, such as witness statements, or possibly certain forensic analyses have to be conducted. After all that, once the preliminary examination is completed, the case file is sent to the public prosecutor who decides whether or not an indictment will be raised. If so, and once the indictment is in force, a court hearing is scheduled. The procedure is continued until the passing of a first instance ruling against which the parties can appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned that the preliminary examination is mandatory if the act committed is punished by five years of imprisonment or more. What about acts which are punished by a lesser punishment?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: When an act is punishable by less than five years, an indictment can be raised without a preliminary examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do describe what an investigating judge can do under this law.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge is authorised to conduct an investigation against a person for whom there is a founded suspicion that he or she has committed a crime. During the investigation, the investigating judge is the only person authorised to collect evidence. During the investigation, the investigating judge has some powers, for example, if he or she doesn't agree with the request of the public prosecutor that an investigation be launched, the investigating judge can express his or her disagreement. In that case, three professional judges will decide about the matter. During the investigation, the investigating judge also decides about the request of the prosecutor to put the suspect into detention, whether there are legal grounds to detain that person and the investigating judge can also disagree or fail to grant that request. During the investigation or, rather, even before it is launched, the investigating judge can conduct certain investigative activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How does one become an investigating judge? In earlier proceedings this question was also raised because it was obviously unclear. Once you became investigating judge, you said that in 1994 you became -- you were assigned to that position. Was a special training required for judges to become investigating judges? Was there a special procedure or anything?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: To do the work of an investigating judge, no special training is required, nor is there a special procedure in place to appoint somebody to become an investigating judge. It's only important that the judge implement the law and know the law. The judge needs a certain amount of experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking about investigations or preliminary examinations, it was also unclear what exactly happens and what is done. Firstly, what are investigative activities? I would like to hear an answer to that. And, secondly, in connection with these investigative activities, can some of these activities be transferred to the police? Does the law provide for that? In which cases is that possible, and how far can that go? And then we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure stipulates that the investigating judge is authorised to conduct certain investigative activities. There are some activities of this type that the judge can conduct during the investigation itself. Such as, summoning the accused and interviewing him or her, interviewing witnesses, conducting forensic analyses, conducting other analyses and on-site investigations that are done by crime techs, and there are also some investigative activities that the investigating judge can transfer to the police. The investigating activities of the latter type are an order to search certain facilities, if necessary to locate the perpetrator of a crime or if necessary to find objects that were used in committing a crime. Likewise, such objects can be taken away from the suspect. A receipt is issued to him or her, and all these activities, these investigative activities, can be transferred to the police before the investigation itself is launched, during the investigation itself. Upon the order of the investigating judge, the police are duty-bound to act if the accused who has been informed but failed to respond to the summons. The police then brings in the suspect upon the order of the investigating judge to be interviewed. The same applies to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: After the decision is taken to conduct an investigation, does the police have any powers with regard to the suspect once he or she is detained?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, the police have no powers from that moment on. Once the decision on conducting an investigation is taken, not only does the police have no powers, but also the public prosecutor has no right to interfere with the work of the investigating judge, although the investigating judge acts upon his or her request to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As there have been doubts with regard to the misuse of rights of investigating judges, let me ask you the following: Under this Law on Criminal Procedure which was in force in the relevant time-period, did the investigating judge have the right under precisely defined conditions to withhold evidence from defence lawyers during the investigation? Tell us all you know about that, please.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge has the right and the powers during the investigation to withhold some rights from the defence counsel of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In which cases is it possible to do that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The law clearly stipulates the conditions for that, namely when the interests of the state are concerned and for security reasons related to defence or the state borders. In such cases, defence counsel can be prevented from reviewing the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the defence counsel were able to review the case file once the indictment was raised?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The law stipulates the time-period required for them to review the file and prepare the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question will refer to the police. Was the investigating judge duty-bound to inform the police about his or her activities?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but there's something else I would like to add. As far as my decision was concerned that I passed during the investigation to prevent the defence counsel from reviewing the case file, the parties to the proceedings had the right to appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember my previous question, were you duty-bound to report to the police on the development of the investigation once the investigation was launched?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I, as an investigating judge, acted independently, and I had -- I was not duty-bound to report to the police or inform them on the development of the investigation. I act upon the request of the public prosecutor, and once the investigation is completed, I return the file to the prosecution. The police has no such rights, nor am I duty-bound to inform them. The police also is not duty-bound to carry out some activities during the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it would be advisable to go into private session now since the witness is about to speak about some events and mention names of some persons we believe should be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we have hitherto spoken of the Law on Criminal Procedure --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, counsel. Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, thank you. I'm sorry, because I'm impatient. [Interpretation] Could 65 ter 1824 that the witness spoke about be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00855.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The next topic which I think we have enough time to deal with is investigations when there is a state of war. Do you know when a state of war was declared, and whether there were any special changes in the Law on Criminal Procedure or something similar? In other words, did the procedure change when a state of war was declared, the one that you followed as an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: A state of war was declared on the 24th of March, 1999, and some ten days later, the federal government issued a decree on the implementation of the Law on Criminal Procedure in war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P200 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at this "Official Gazette," look at the provisions. Is this the decree on implementing the Law on Criminal Procedure during the state of war that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the decree issued on the 24th of April, 1999, and it entered into force the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment briefly on the process rights of the investigating judge that were changed, what the position of the accused, the prosecutor, the police was. Please explain.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here 24th of April, I think it should be -- or, rather, the translation says the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your remark is quite correct. It's the 4th of April, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is not the original the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says the 24th on the copy I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question, which was, what changes did this decree introduce?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the state of war and the difficult conditions of work, this decree provided for the investigating judge and the organs of the interior to be able to carry out certain investigative activities even without authorisation from the public prosecutor if the matter was urgent, but they had to inform the public prosecutor immediately. So that even without a request from the public prosecutor, the investigating judge was authorised to conduct an investigation to carry out an on-site investigation without the authorisation and presence of the public prosecutor. And as regards detention or remanding people in custody, the investigating judge and the organs of the interior could detain a person who was a suspect for up to a month. This decree also shortened the dead-lines after the prosecutor raised an indictment as regards the right to appeal and the procedure on deciding on these appeals was also cut short, so as to enable a speedier trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And the right to file an indictment without the participation of an investigating judge, did this change?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The public prosecutor was authorised to file an indictment directly for crimes involving a minimum sentence of up to five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is as follows: There were two investigating judges in the district court in Pristina. There were also times when there were three or four investigating judges. How were cases assigned to a particular judge? Were there judges dealing with special kinds of cases, or was another principle applied when assigning cases? Of course, it's understandable if there are only two judges, they would take cases in alternate -- in an alternating way. But what about when there were more than two judges?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when the situation was normal, according to the rules of the procedure of court, the cases were assigned in the order they arrived, in the order that the judges had, so one could not influence the assignment of cases and every judge would get the next case that arrived. So all four of us would get one case, and then the first person would get the fifth case, so the consecutive order would be followed. The clerk assigning the cases knew this. So it didn't matter what the case was about, what the persons involved were, who they were, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any exceptions to this rule?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were exceptions. When an investigating judge was on duty there were four of us, and each one of us would do duty on one Sunday in each month, because there would be four Sundays in a month. So when one of us was on duty, any urgent cases that had to do with remanding someone in custody or carrying out an on-site investigation would take the case, and would keep the case, carry on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the only exception to the rule?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And how was it in war time? As of the 24th of March, 1999, until around the 15th of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, as there were only two investigating judges left, we took cases according to who had more time at the moment. If I had set out to interview witnesses, for example, and an on-site investigation had to be carried out at the same time, my colleague would do it. Sometimes you would have to go to two places at once, and then he would go to one location and I would go to the other. So we had to act urgently according to priorities, and we didn't pay attention to the consecutive order that the cases arrived in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question in this set of questions before we take the break will be as follows: Tell the Chamber what was the territorial jurisdiction of the district court in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The territorial jurisdiction of the district court covered a certain territory, and if a crime was committed on that territory, it would be the district court that would have jurisdiction over the perpetrators. The territorial jurisdiction of the district court in Pristina covered a certain number of municipalities. We had jurisdiction over cases in the territories of the municipalities of Pristina, Lipljan, Urosevac, Djeneral Jankovic, Kacanik, and Novo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before we take the break, my last question in this set: Were there any exceptions to this rule? Did you carry on on-site investigations outside the territorial jurisdiction of your court, was that possible?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that was not possible. Each -- there were actually five, Prizren, Pec, Kosovska Mitrovica, Pristina, so there were five district courts, and each one was responsible for its own territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So your answer is no?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my last question before the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. We must have a break now to rewind tapes. We resume in half an hour at 11.00. A Court Officer will assist you during the breaks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we now please have P50 on our monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will now have this question for you. Based on what material law was -- were the decisions, court rulings made at the time in question, the relevant period, what were the criminal law provisions that applied?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, speaking about the relevant period, the law that was in force, what I see in front of me now, is the criminal law of Serbia, of the Republic of Serbia, and there was another Criminal Code, the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Criminal Code of Serbia is what we have in front of us; right?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see P1370 so that the witness can confirm whether that was the other law was that was in force. In other words, P1370.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the Criminal Code of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now we can move on. Now, tell us, please, what is the difference -- or what was the difference, rather, between these two codes? Were they in parallel, were they in competition, or were they actually complementary? Could you just give us a brief description.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: These two Criminal Codes were not in competition or mutually exclusive. The Criminal Code of Yugoslavia -- other than providing the general provisions relating to crimes and criminal sanctions, the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia provided for the crimes that related to the constitutional order of Yugoslavia, the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia, the crimes relating to enemy activities, creation of enemy organisations, and involvement or engagement in enemy activity. In other words, everything that was against the constitutional order of Yugoslavia and the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia as a whole. The Criminal Code of Serbia regulated matters that dealt with individual crimes of a general character.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. My next question is this, and this will bring us close to the completion of this important area, and relates to the laws in the relevant period. My question would have to do with the substantive jurisdiction, subject matter jurisdiction, and what the relationship was between the regular courts and the military courts, both during and before and after the NATO campaign.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The subject matter distribution -- jurisdiction of the regular courts, the lower courts and the district courts, was that in they dealt with the crimes regardless of the perpetrator. Whereas the district court actually had the subject matter the jurisdiction for all crimes that envisaged a sentence of over ten years, where the minimum penalty would be a ten-year sentence and over. As for military courts, as far as I can recall now, although I'm not very familiar with that area, the military courts had jurisdiction over all crimes that related to the Army of Yugoslavia and those crimes that were committed by military personnel. It was a special law that pertained to -- or a special code that pertained to a specific -- to specific criminal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us that some of your colleagues, if I'm not mistaken, actually began working as investigating judges for military courts once the state of war was declared.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after the state of war was declared, military courts were established, their jurisdiction was defined, and judges from the general courts, courts with a general jurisdiction, were taken over by them and they were appointed as military judges and military prosecutors, so that the district court of Pristina, for instance, had some of their judges that dealt with the criminal -- with crimes actually transferred to military courts and some of them also became military prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And that is one of the reasons why the number of judges in the Pristina court actually went down; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question to do with this is this: You've already mentioned that your work was far greater now that the NATO campaign started because you had some additional matters to deal with including damages and offences that dealt with or were related to the NATO campaign. Now, my question will relate specifically to a crime, a great increase in a certain type of crime which was the crime of the offences against the territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Could you tell us something about this type of crime?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: When speaking of this criminal offence, forming an organisation in order to engage in enemy activity, the first time that I came across this type of crime was -- and that I dealt with it and investigated it as an investigating judge was in 1994. From that time onwards, although there were instances even before that where we had to adjudicate in these types of crimes, but these were then conducted by a colleague of mine, this was before I actually became an investigating judge, but after this period, this type of crimes increased so that all investigating judges who were in the investigations department had to deal with this type of crime both in the district courts in Pristina as well as in other district courts in Kosovo and Metohija. The number of such criminal offences increased both before the war and during the war-time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. To wrap up this topic, could you please tell me, what do you know about the difficulties that you had in conducting investigations during the war time and immediately preceding the war time? I'm actually referring to difficulties that you encountered in the conduct of your official duties. Did you have any problems that had to deal directly with your work? Or perhaps you know of some problems that your colleagues encountered in the discharge of their duties. Could you tell us something about it.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: When speaking about our work in war time, both my colleagues and I who remained at the court, both the district and the lower courts, we encountered difficulties because there was fear and panic around us. And very frequently there were cases where NATO aircraft bombed or dropped bombs, and while we were working in the courthouses we could hear nearby the blasts, the explosions. There was panic among the employees, so we had difficulties, for example, ensuring that there is a court reporter, that there is an interpreter in the courtroom. There was also a difficulty sometimes to ensure that there was defence counsel in instances where they had to be assigned, and there were even instances where, for instance I had this, where one night when I set off to conduct an on-site investigation, we actually went the wrong way and we hit an ambush where there were terrorists who had set it. Fortunately we managed to avoid fatal consequences because the operative, the crime technician who was with me could speak Albanian, and we happened to be in a civilian vehicle so that we managed to actually avoid being killed. On the ground, we found and saw many dead people who were killed during the NATO bombing campaign. And even as we were conducting on-site investigations, we could hear the air-raid alarms going off. However, even in such difficult circumstances -- something is off, something was switched off. Well, even though the circumstances were so difficult, my colleagues and I did our best to do our job properly, to do our jobs, to actually keep a record of all such cases and conduct them to the end completing all the measures that we were supposed to do during -- by law, including the investigation, examination, identification of bodies. And everything else that we were able to do in view of the circumstances and the risk that the circumstances posed to all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, did you ever learn, did you have any knowledge about your life being actually at risk? Did you ever learn that you were in danger?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, threats were issued both in writing and by telephone. And in one of the cases that I worked on against the group of terrorists, one of the accused, among other things, mentioned during his testimony that a group of terrorists that was active in Pristina had planned to execute me as an investigating judge, and he mentioned the name of this investigating judge unaware that actually it was me. And when the prosecutor asked this accused what the reason was and why they wanted to execute this investigating judge, he said that he didn't know, but that he was assigned the task of following me to find out my movements, my normal movements, because the person who was supposed to execute me was to be provided all this -- all these details; whereas his task was just to find out my movements during the day. When he learned that the investigating judge in question was, in fact, me, he began to apologise, and he said to me, Thank God I didn't take part in anything like that, because I can see now that all you are doing is you are doing your job, and there would have been no sense to execute you. The person who was supposed to execute me was soon involved in an incident with a police where he opened fire on a police patrol, and he was killed in this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Marinkovic, you were an investigating judge in the Pristina district court in 1997 and 1998, the years preceding the war in Kosovo and Metohija. At this time, in other words, before the events that followed in 1999, were there instances where civilians of Albanian or non-Albanian descent were attacked? Were there attacks on police stations or other government institutions?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would appreciate it if the binder with the exhibits may be provided to the witness so that we can actually move through them more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could we now please pull up 65 ter D007-2620.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, Mrs. Marinkovic, this exhibit is marked under tab 3, so you may take a look at it. Now you have it before you on the screen as well. Please take a look at this document and tell us, we see that this is from the period preceding the NATO bombing campaign in Kosovo and Metohija. Could you tell us something more about this incident. What is it that we are looking at when we look at this document?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: What we see here is an official document. It bears number 36/97. This is an on-site investigation report which I conducted as an investigating judge, and I also drafted this on site investigation report on the 16th of January, 1997. The on-site investigation was conducted regarding -- or into the circumstances or incident in Pristina on the 16th of January, 1997, in Vojvode Zivojina Misica Street where a car bomb had exploded. The report also states all the persons present during the on-site investigation. The deputy district public prosecutor, Jovica Jovanovic is named; the Pristina SUP inspector, Srecko Stevanovic; and the crime investigator or officer, Jankovic, Nenad. They were members of the investigative team who always attended crime scenes when an on-site investigation had to be conducted. The investigation was conducted by the investigating judge. The criminal technician was there to assist in drawing up a sketch of the crime scene to fix the trace evidence and do all the necessary measurements on the crime scene. On that day when this car bomb exploded there was a huge blast and it was later established that the explosive that was used was of -- was very strong. And as I lived on the same street, we all heard this explosion. This actually instilled fear and panic, panic amongst all of us because we didn't know what was going on. This explosive was planted in a passenger car that the -- Mr. Radivoje Popovic, the dean of the Pristina university drove, and on that occasion when the car bomb exploded, the man was seriously wounded as was his driver. In this on-site investigation report, all my observations are stated, everything that I established, and it says here that the vehicles in the immediate vicinity were damaged, and the vehicle in which the dean and his driver were was completely destroyed. They were immediately taken to Pristina Clinical Hospital so that -- or, rather, this event was the first of its kind in Pristina. This was a kind of terrorist attack in which a car bomb exploded. It was directed against Dean Popovic who at the time advocated in the interests of the university, and he was opposed to the idea that an illegal university be established as a parallel institution to the official one. That's something on which some Albanians insisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thanks. That will be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00856.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next Defence document is D007-0664. Could we please see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, madam, you will see it under tab 4. Thank you, now you can see it. My question is the same as the one about the first document. You have explained the role of the crime technicians and all the other persons present, let us now focus on what you drafted here, what kind of event this was and what consequences did it have, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This is also an official document. It is filed under number 115/97. It's an on-site investigation report made on the 18th of November, 1997. The on-site investigation was conducted in the village of Komorane after a terrorist attack was carried out against Camilj Gasi and Eljmi Bubljaku, both from Komorane. This terrorist attack was directed against Albanians who continued working in the government institutions of the Republic of Serbia. They ignored the recommendation of that they boycott the Serbian institutions. Camilj Gasi was a director of the socially-owned company in Glogovac municipality, and he was also a federal member of parliament at the time. Eljmi Bubljaku was his driver. And they were ambushed and shot at. Camilj Gasi was wounded, and this report states that cartridges were found at the site, as well as bullet-holes in the vehicle. Camilj was wounded in the right thigh and in the neck by bullets. We secured all the traces at the site. The site was photographed and sketched by hand, and this report was sent to the public prosecutor who received one copy and another copy went to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you a question that I will repeat with regard to every subsequent document about incidents where people came to harm. Were the perpetrators found? The perpetrators of this crime or the previous one.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the previous one, the car bomb where Mr. Popovic was wounded, during the investigation the perpetrator as well as the organiser and those who planned it were found. And a first instance ruling was passed which was confirmed after an appeal. And the second instance, the perpetrator was not found. Remained unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00857.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence moves that Exhibit D -- or, rather, document D007-2624 be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Marinkovic, it's under tab 5 in your binder. Here we have both documents, so my question is the same as previously.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This is also a report that I drafted as an investigating judge. This has to do with the on-site investigation conducted on the 29th of November, 1997, in Petrastica village in the Stimlje municipality. When a terrorist attack was carried out against Dalip Dugoli who died of the consequences of the injuries sustained. He worked for the agricultural cooperative in Stimlje. This is a classical example of a terrorist attack on an Albanian civilian. He was attacked because he worked for the agricultural cooperative of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The perpetrators were not found. He was shot at right outside the yard when he was entering the yard with his vehicle. He was found by his brother Tefik and his cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00858.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also please see document D007-2628 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 6 in your binders, madam. Same question again.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This is also an on-site investigation report. The investigation was conducted on the 12th of January, 1998, when a building was attacked in which the families of police officers who worked at the Stimlje police station had accommodation. The record number of this document is 2/98. The report states what was found at the site. It's the building of the former primary school which was adapted for housing purposes for police officers' families. On that day, several bullet-holes were found in the building. The walls were damaged. Six families of police officers lived there, that is their wives and young children. There were bursts of fire from a hill shot at the building, and a number of cartridges were found on that hill. The calibre was 7.62 millimetres. These were collected for the crime techs to inspect them. There was only material damage done, but no persons came to harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were the perpetrators discovered?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00859.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document we would like to see on the screen is D007-2632.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Marinkovic, this is tab 7 in your binder. We can see both versions on the screen.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In this on-site investigation report which I drafted as investigating judge, deals with an incident that happened on the 12th of January, 1998, when Sejdi Muja a forester from the village of Gradica was murdered. He was shot at on that morning when he left to go to work because he worked in Glogovac for the forestry state there. I can say that it was already very risky for our personal -- for reasons that had to do our personal security to go to on-site investigations because terrorist gangs were roaming about, and they would fire without warning. They would ambush people. We found 28 cartridges of 7.62 millimetre calibre fired from automatic weapons. The victim sustained grave injuries and died of these injuries. He was attacked because he worked for the public or state-owned company of Serbian forests in Glogovac. He refused to boycott Serbian government institutions as ordered by the KLA. His neighbour, Selimun Dibrani [phoen] was with him on that morning, but that neighbour wasn't harmed. He stated that he noticed that morning that the deceased was approached by three masked persons. They wore stockings over their faces with openings for the eyes. They were armed with automatic weapons and they approached the victim and said, Stop. And they sent the neighbour home, saying, Don't turn around. The body was sent to the forensic medicine institute where an autopsy was conducted to establish the cause of death. Crime site was photographed and sketches were made by hand. The file was forwarded to the public prosecutor, but unfortunately, the perpetrators of this crime were never found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00860.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also ask that D007, be brought up on the screen, slash 2636.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, madam, it's number 8, tab number 8.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I drew up this report, the official number is Kri number 8/98. It refers to an event that occurred on the 27th of January, 1998, in Urosevac, in the town itself, when an explosive device was thrown on a house belonging to Sinisa Marjanovic from the yard of the house. The attack was aimed at him because he had a tenant called Rajko Doder, an employee of the Urosevac SUP. No one was hurt, but there was material damage to parts of the house. On site we found pieces of shrapnel. In the yard we found a crater, 24 by 40 centimetres -- or, rather, 40 by 40 centimetres, and its depth was 20 centimetres. This terrorist attack targeted a member of the MUP. Fortunately no one was injured or killed. But this event caused feelings of insecurity and fear among the population. In this period with frequent terrorist attacks against Albanian civilians and non-Albanians, police officers and so on, non-Serbs began to -- or, rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Non-Albanians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretaiton] Serbs and others began moving out of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00861.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have D007-2640 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's number 9 in your binder, madam.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report on an on-site investigation which I drew up concerning an event that occurred on the 28th of January, 1998, in the village of Sibovac in Obilic municipality where the family of Dragomir Spasic lives and that whose house a shell from a hand-held launcher was fired. This terrorist attack was aimed at this family because Dragomir Spasic's son was an employee of the police, Momir Spasic was an employee of the Urosevac SUP. I wish to add in connection with this event, while we carried out an on-site investigation late at night, and this was very risky for us because there were frequent terrorist attacks and one never knew where and when fire might be opened. However, as the authorised investigating judge, I told the rest of the team that we would in fact carry out the on-site investigation in spite of the risk because I knew that the family were afraid. They were surrounded by Albanian houses, and I was concerned about them because if they were left to their own devices the whole night, they would be even more afraid, so I wanted to reassure that family by arriving there and carrying out an on-site investigation, drawing up a report, and assuring them that the court would do whatever was necessary to find the perpetrators. According to what they said that evening, they heard a strong explosion. Everything in the house shook and rattled. They didn't know what was going on. They immediately reported this to the duty service of the interior. I heard about this from them, and set out to carry out an on-site investigation. I was accompanied by the deputy of the district public prosecutor and the rest of the team, but that evening for reasons of security the chief and a team of policemen escorted us to make sure we could carry out the on-site investigation without hindrance and to ensure our security. No one was killed here, but there was large-scale material damage and we found shells from a hand-held launcher which we kept for further forensic analysis. The perpetrators of this terrorist attack were not found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00862.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is D007-2644.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's tab 10, madam.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: What I see on the screen and under tab 9A --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, it is 9A, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report which I drew up on the 13th of February, 1998, concerning a terrorist attack on a postman, Mustafa Kurtaj from the village of Gornje Obrinje, Glogovac municipality. He died of his injuries. I wish to stress that it was risky to go to this area because according to operative information, both the prosecutor and I knew that members of the KLA were active in the area. We carried out the on-site investigation in the morning. We arrived on the site at 9.00 a.m. We carried out the investigation as fast as we could in order to be able to return as soon as possible. The body of Mustafa Kurtaj was found at the bus-stop of the bus going from Gornje Obrinje to Glogovac. He had been on his way to work because he worked as a postman in the post office in Glogovac. On the site we found 27 spent cartridges of automatic weapons. The deceased had injuries to his head which was blown apart, and we found a piece of his skull nearby. There were also injuries to his stomach, chest, and head, and there were traces of the projectile in his clothing in the area of the head. I ordered an autopsy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to pause, please. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wonder if this document was notified because I'm not able to find it on our notification from the Defence. Perhaps Mr. Djordjevic can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend, that is D007-2644. It is are on the monitor right now. I checked, it's 65 ter 205 and 339. D 65 ter, as I said, 205 and 339. There are two numbers because the document in fact, appears twice. There are two copies of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please continue, Mrs. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Mustafa Kurtaj was an Albanian, a civilian who was killed because he worked in a post office which was a state institution of the Republic of Serbia, and he did not want to join the KLA terrorist gang. We learned this because his brother worked at Pristina airport, and he was later interviewed, and he said that they had had frequent visits and threats if they did not support the ideas of the KLA. They were told they would have to bear the consequences. The perpetrator of this terrorist attack was unfortunately never discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00863.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is D007-2648. Could we have it on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, it's tab 10. Mrs. Marinkovic, please go ahead as soon as the document shows up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an on-site investigation report, an official document, number Kri number 38/98. I compiled it and signed it as the investigating judge, and it concerns an attack carried out on the 14th of April, 1998, on the second police station of the Vranjevac department, Vranjevac neighbourhood, Pristina municipality. On site we discovered that the attack was carried out with an explosive device. We established that there was severe damage to the building of the police station, that this had occurred on the previous day between 2300 and 2330 hours, according to what the policemen on duty told us. Besides the damage to the house, there was also damage to a vehicle parked in the yard. We found parts of an explosive device which the ballistics expert who was in the team found to be from a hand-grenade. On that occasion, policeman Budimir Spasic was injured. He had injuries to his left hand and left temple. Parts of the hand-grenade and a piece of shrapnel were taken from the site for further forensic investigation. The injured policemen was born in 1962, was given immediate medical assistance, and was taken to the hospital in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, were the perpetrators found?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How densely populated is this area, Vranjevac in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this neighbourhood is populated mainly with ethnic Albanians. There are many private homes there, and the police station building is right next to the road on the right-hand side as you go from Pristina in the direction of Podujevo. People living in the immediate vicinity heard the explosion. They were afraid, and a feeling of fear and insecurity was created, especially now that the police station had been attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We see from the report at what time of day the on-site investigation was carried out. When did the actual explosion take place?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as it says here in the report, on the 13th of April, 1998, at about 2330 hours. However, we could not carry out the on-site investigation immediately; we did it the next morning for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00864.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we now have D007-2654.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, it's tab 11, Mrs. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an on-site investigation report filed under number Kri 49/98 compiled on the 12th of May, 1998, when an on-site investigation was carried out after a terrorist attack on members of the MUP of Serbia in Pristina. The attack was carried out at the address Ljubotenska Street 17 which is in the centre of town, an urban area. It was carried out in the morning, and fire was opened from a house. When I carried out the on-site investigation after this event, in front of the house from which shots were fired, we found many spent shell casings, 28 pistol cartridges, and when searching the house, we found a large quantity of weapons. The report lists all the weapons found.
